sections.h2: What kind of city is Helena?
sections.html:
Helena is the capital of Montana and the county seat of Lewis and Clark County. The 2020 census counted 32,091 residents, which made it the sixth most populous city in the state and the fifth least populous state capital in the country. The Helena metro area, covering Lewis and Clark and Jefferson counties, had 83,058 people.

The city covers about 17 square miles and is served by Helena Regional Airport. It sits in the Helena Valley, with Tenmile Creek running through town and hillside neighborhoods rising on the edges. That hillside setting matters when you sell, because slopes, access roads and fire exposure are part of how a buyer sees a lot.

sections.h2: How did a gold camp become the state capital?
sections.html:
Helena began as a gold camp. Gold was found at Last Chance Gulch on July 14, 1864, and the town was formally established on October 30, 1864. The wealth of the early years left a mark on the housing stock: by 1888 about 50 millionaires lived in the area, and the concentration of money produced the elaborate Victorian architecture the city is known for.

Helena has been the capital of Montana Territory since 1875 and of the state since 1889, and voters kept it there in referendums in 1892 and 1894. The Montana State Capitol was completed in 1902. Downtown's walking mall follows the original path of Last Chance Gulch. It was built in the early 1980s after urban renewal removed many historic buildings from the downtown district.

Government is the base of the local economy, and that tends to give Helena steadier employment than many Montana towns. Roughly 18 percent of working Helenans work for state government agencies, and the city is also a hub of county and federal activity. Education is a large employer too, with two high schools, their elementary and middle schools, and Helena College. Carroll College and the medical community are the major private employers listed for the city.

What does that mean for a seller? Buyers in Helena often have ties to government, schools or health care. An owner who relocates for work, retires or inherits a house from a parent often needs a predictable closing date, which is worth raising with any buyer.

sections.h2: What is Helena's climate, and how does it affect a house?
sections.html:
Helena has a semi-arid climate with long, cold winters, hot dry summers and short springs and autumns. Precipitation averages only 11.4 inches a year and mostly falls in spring. Snow can fall in any month except July but normally accumulates in light amounts, and chinook winds bring warm spells in winter.

The temperature range is wide. Helena has recorded 105 degrees Fahrenheit and a low of minus 42. With swings that wide, expect a buyer's inspector to look closely at the roof, siding and foundation.

Earthquakes are part of the local record as well. The 1935 Helena earthquake damaged the Broadwater Natatorium, which closed in 1941.

sections.h2: What do Helena's zoning rules say about fire, slopes and accessory units?
sections.html:
The city's zoning code states that its regulations seek to minimize danger from wildland fires, stormwater flooding, soil erosion and other environmental hazards, to mitigate traffic hazards and to protect the scenic character of hillside areas. Chapter 2 of Title 11 of the Helena City Code sets out the land uses allowed in each district.

The same chapter covers accessory dwelling units. An ADU is allowed accessory to a single-dwelling unit residence only, with one per lot. A detached or attached ADU cannot exceed 75 percent of the square footage of the main house or 1,000 square feet, whichever is less. If your property has a garage apartment or a converted basement, check with the city that it was permitted and fits these limits, because an unpermitted unit has to be disclosed.

For a sale, here is a simple checklist:

  • Confirm the zoning district of your lot on the city's planning pages.
  • Find permits for additions, finished basements and any second unit.
  • Note any hillside, drainage or access issues you know of.
  • Collect records for roof, furnace and chimney work.

sections.h2: Who handles building permits and historic review in Helena?
sections.html:
The City of Helena's Community Development Department. Its Building Division conducts building and site plan reviews, issues building permits and provides inspections within the city limits. Historic Preservation is housed in the same department.

If you remodeled without permits, a buyer may ask the city for records, and a missing permit can slow a deal. Montana's disclosure law asks sellers to say whether substantial additions or alterations were made without a building permit. It is better to deal with that before the contract than after.

sections.h2: How and when are Helena property taxes paid?
sections.html:
Lewis and Clark County collects the tax. Real property tax bills are mailed by the county treasurer, usually in late October, and the first payment is due November 30 or within 30 days of the postmark, whichever is later, with the second due May 31. The county processes about 37,000 real estate tax bills each year.

Payments go to Lewis and Clark County at 316 North Park Avenue, Room 113, Helena, and the property tax office can be reached at 406-447-8329. Under the tiered rates that began with tax year 2025, the first $400,000 of a home's market value is taxed at 0.76 percent, the part up to $1.5 million at 1.10 percent and anything above that at 2.20 percent, according to the Department of Revenue.

At closing, the title company settles whatever tax is owed for the current period out of your proceeds.

sections.h2: What must a Montana seller disclose?
sections.html:
You must give the buyer a written statement of adverse material facts you actually know. Section 70-20-502 of the Montana Code includes matters of title, water and wastewater, utilities, structural and mechanical systems, soil and drainage problems, and any testing for radon, mold, lead-based paint or contaminated soil. If the statement is delivered after a contract is signed, the buyer has three days to rescind under section 70-20-504.

Exemptions in section 70-20-503 include court-ordered transfers such as probate, foreclosure sales and transfers to a spouse, child or parent.

sections.h2: What are your options if you need to sell a Helena house?
sections.html:
• List with an agent. The house is exposed to the full market, with showings and a buyer's inspection and loan to work through.
  • Sell on your own. There is no commission, but you manage the buyer, the contract and the disclosure yourself.
  • Accept a cash offer. The buyer purchases as-is, and there is no loan approval to wait on. The offer takes account of the condition of the house, so ask for it in writing and compare your net.

Whatever the route, request a payoff statement for your mortgage and any liens, and an estimate of closing costs, so you know what is left.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit record to sell my Helena house?
faqs.a: Montana's disclosure statement asks about additions made without a building permit. Contact the city's Building Division to check what is on file.

faqs.q: How many accessory dwelling units can I have on a Helena lot?
faqs.a: One. The city code allows one ADU per lot, accessory to a single-dwelling unit residence, and limits it to 75 percent of the main house or 1,000 square feet, whichever is less.

faqs.q: When are Lewis and Clark County property taxes due?
faqs.a: The first half is due on November 30, or within 30 days of the postmark if that is later. The second half is due May 31.

faqs.q: Is Helena in a wildfire area?
faqs.a: The city's zoning code says its regulations seek to minimize danger from wildland fires, which tells you fire exposure is a planning concern, especially on hillsides. Ask your insurer and the city about your specific address.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Helena house that I inherited?
faqs.a: Yes, once the person with legal authority over the estate can sign. Transfers ordered by a probate court are exempt from the seller disclosure statement under section 70-20-503.
